title: Homework time in online and in-person sections

stimulus.title: Weekly homework time by course format
stimulus.text: A large university offers its introductory economics course in two formats, online and in person. An administrator selected an independent random sample of students from each format (from the hundreds enrolled in each) and asked how many hours they spent on homework for the course last week (invented data). Graphs of both samples show moderate right skew and no outliers. The administrator wants to know whether online students spend more time on homework, on average.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses for the administrator's question, and define any parameters you use.

rubric.point: Correct hypotheses with parameters: H_0: mu_O - mu_I = 0 and H_a: mu_O - mu_I > 0 (or mu_O = mu_I and mu_O > mu_I).
accept: H_0: mu_1 = mu_2, H_a: mu_1 > mu_2 with 1 = online
H_0: mu_O - mu_I = 0, H_a: mu_O - mu_I > 0

rubric.point: Defines both parameters in context: the true mean weekly homework hours of all students in the online section and of all students in the in-person section.
accept: mu_O = true mean hours of homework per week for all online students in the course
population mean homework time for each format

parts.sample: H_0: mu_O - mu_I = 0, H_a: mu_O - mu_I > 0, where mu_O is the true mean hours of homework last week for all students in the online format and mu_I is the true mean for all students in the in-person format.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate test by name and verify that its conditions are met.

rubric.point: Names a two-sample t test for a difference of means (not paired, not a z test for proportions).
accept: two-sample t test for mu_O - mu_I
two-sample t test using s_O and s_I separately

rubric.point: Random and 10%: independent random samples from each format, and 38 and 42 are each less than 10% of the hundreds of students in their format.
accept: random samples of each format; 38 < 10% of online students, 42 < 10% of in-person students

rubric.point: Normal/large sample: both samples have n of at least 30 (38 and 42), so the sampling distribution of the difference is approximately normal despite the moderate skew.
accept: both samples are large, by the central limit theorem

parts.sample: Two-sample t test for mu_O - mu_I. Random: independent random samples of online and in-person students. 10%: 38 is less than 10% of the online students and 42 is less than 10% of the in-person students. Normal/large sample: n_O = 38 >= 30 and n_I = 42 >= 30, so the moderate skew is not a problem.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and the p-value. Show your work.

rubric.point: Shows the formula with values substituted: t = (7.9 - 6.6)/sqrt(3.1^2/38 + 2.7^2/42).
Gives the p-value, about 0.025, with df stated (technology df 73.8, or conservative df 37 with p about 0.027; Table B bracket between 0.025 and 0.05 also earns the point).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State the conclusion of the test at the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ in context. Then explain whether the administrator can conclude that the online format causes students to spend more time on homework.

rubric.point: Conclusion linked to the p-value and alpha, in context: because 0.025 < 0.05, reject H_0; there is convincing evidence that the true mean weekly homework time is greater for online students than for in-person students.
accept: p = 0.025 < 0.05, reject H_0, convincing evidence that mu_O > mu_I in context

rubric.point: Scope: no, because students were not randomly assigned to formats (an observational study); students who choose online sections may differ in other ways. The random samples do allow generalizing to the students in each format.
accept: no cause and effect without random assignment
observational study, so only an association

parts.sample: Because the p-value of 0.025 is less than alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the true mean weekly homework time is greater for online students than for in-person students in this course. The administrator cannot conclude that the format causes the difference, because students chose their format rather than being randomly assigned; for example, online students may have different schedules or backgrounds. The random samples do let the result be generalized to all students in each format.
